item.title: [Logistics 101 #5] Stop Treating Every Item on the Shelf the Same
item.body:
> Inventory isn't one problem — it's four questions: which items matter most, how little you can hold, who does the reordering, and how fast the whole pile moves.

## Today's Concept

Every business that stocks anything faces the same tension. Hold too much, and cash sits on a shelf getting dusty (and paying rent). Hold too little, and you turn customers away.

The instinct is to solve this once, for everything. That's the mistake. A hardware store carries $80 cordless drills and 3-cent washers in the same building. Counting them with the same care is a waste of somebody's afternoon.

Four tools handle this, and they stack:

**1. ABC analysis — decide where to spend attention.**
Rank every item by *annual dollar volume* (unit cost × units used per year), then split the list into three buckets. In a typical operation the pattern looks roughly like this:

- **A items:** ~20% of the items, ~80% of the dollars. Watch closely, count often, forecast carefully.
- **B items:** ~30% of the items, ~15% of the dollars. Moderate control.
- **C items:** ~50% of the items, ~5% of the dollars. Order big, order rarely, don't agonize.

Those percentages are a rule of thumb (the Pareto principle), not a law — your actual curve might be 15/85 or 30/70. The point stands either way: attention is scarce, so aim it at the A items.

One caveat that trips people up: dollar volume isn't the only thing that matters. A 3-cent gasket that shuts down a production line is a C item by cost and an A item by consequence. Good practice is to override the ranking for anything that's critical, hard to source, or has a long lead time.

**2. JIT (Just-In-Time) — shrink what you hold.**
Developed inside Toyota's production system, JIT means material arrives right when it's needed, in the quantity needed. Instead of forecasting demand and pushing inventory forward, downstream consumption *pulls* the next delivery.

The payoff is real: less cash tied up, less warehouse space, and defects surface fast because there's no buffer of bad parts to hide behind. The cost is equally real: JIT trades inventory buffer for supply-chain reliability. When something breaks upstream — a port backup, a chip shortage, a snowstorm on I-80 — you feel it in days, not months. That's why many firms after 2020 shifted toward "just-in-case" hybrids: JIT for stable, high-volume items; deliberate buffers for anything single-sourced or coming from far away.

**3. VMI (Vendor-Managed Inventory) — hand the reordering to the supplier.**
Normally the buyer decides when to reorder. Under VMI, the buyer shares actual sales and stock data, and the *supplier* decides what to ship and when, within agreed min/max levels. Walmart and P&G built the best-known version of this in the late 1980s.

Why it helps: the supplier finally sees real demand instead of guessing from lumpy purchase orders. That damps the *bullwhip effect* — the way small wiggles in retail demand get amplified into wild swings in factory orders as they travel upstream. Ownership of the goods may or may not transfer at delivery; that's a contract detail worth pinning down, because it decides who eats the cost of unsold stock.

**4. Inventory turnover — measure whether any of it is working.**

```
Inventory Turnover = Cost of Goods Sold ÷ Average Inventory
Days of Inventory   = 365 ÷ Inventory Turnover
```

Turnover says how many times per year you sell through and replace your entire stock. Use COGS, not revenue — revenue includes your margin, inventory is carried at cost, and mixing them inflates the number.

Higher is generally better, but not infinitely. Turnover that's climbing while stockouts are also climbing means you've gone too lean. And the "good" number is entirely industry-specific: a grocery chain may turn 12–15 times a year, a jeweler 1–2. Compare yourself to your own trend and your own sector, never to a headline benchmark from a different business.

## In Everyday Life

Picture a three-location coffee shop in Austin. Annual COGS is $180,000, and average inventory on hand is $15,000.

```
Turnover = 180,000 ÷ 15,000 = 12 times per year
Days of inventory = 365 ÷ 12 ≈ 30 days
```

Thirty days of stock — for a business selling milk and pastries. Something's off, and ABC analysis shows where. Espresso beans and oat milk are the **A items**: high cost, high volume, and they go stale. Flavored syrups are **B**. Cups, lids, sleeves, and napkins are **C** — thousands of units, a few hundred dollars.

So the owner splits the strategy. Beans move to near-JIT: twice-weekly roaster deliveries sized to last week's actual pours, plus a small safety buffer for the Saturday rush. Pastries were already JIT — the bakery drops them at 5 a.m. daily. Cups go the other way: one big quarterly order, because the storage closet is cheaper than the hassle of reordering.

And that rack of chips and bottled drinks by the register? The distributor's driver already walks in, eyeballs the shelf, and restocks it without anyone at the shop writing a purchase order. That's **VMI** — the same arrangement behind the vendor rep stocking the snack aisle at your local supermarket. The shop stopped counting those items entirely.

Six months later: average inventory is $10,000, turnover is 18, days of inventory is about 20. Roughly $5,000 in cash walked off the shelf and back into the register — and the espresso never ran out.

## Three-Line Recap

1. **ABC analysis** ranks items by annual dollar volume so your attention goes to the 20% of items carrying 80% of the money — with manual overrides for anything mission-critical.
2. **JIT** replaces stock with reliable, frequent replenishment; **VMI** hands the reorder decision to a supplier who can finally see real demand.
3. **Inventory turnover (COGS ÷ average inventory)** is the scoreboard — read it alongside stockout rate, because "faster" is only better until customers start leaving empty-handed.

## ✅ Self Quiz

**Q1.** A distributor stocks 1,000 SKUs. Which items should get the tightest cycle counting and forecasting?
- (a) The 500 SKUs with the highest unit count
- (b) The ~200 SKUs representing about 80% of annual dollar volume
- (c) The cheapest SKUs, since errors there are easy to fix
- (d) Every SKU equally, for fairness

**Q2.** A company reports COGS of $600,000 and average inventory of $50,000. What is inventory turnover, and roughly how many days of stock is that?

**Q3.** O/X — Under Vendor-Managed Inventory, the buyer keeps issuing the purchase orders and the supplier simply ships faster.

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **ABC Analysis** — Classifying inventory into A/B/C tiers by annual dollar volume so control effort matches financial impact.
- **JIT (Just-In-Time)** — A pull-based replenishment approach where material arrives only as it's needed, minimizing held stock at the cost of higher exposure to supply disruption.
- **VMI (Vendor-Managed Inventory)** — An arrangement where the supplier, using shared demand and stock data, decides replenishment timing and quantity within agreed limits.
- **Inventory Turnover** — COGS divided by average inventory; how many times a year stock is sold and replaced.
- **Safety Stock** — Extra inventory held to absorb demand variability and supplier delay; the deliberate buffer that JIT tries to shrink but rarely eliminates.
- **Bullwhip Effect** — The amplification of demand swings as orders move upstream through a supply chain, driven by delayed and distorted information.

---

*Answers:*
*Q1 — (b). ABC ranks by annual dollar volume (unit cost × annual usage), not unit count or unit price alone. The A tier is where tight control pays for itself. Just remember the override: a cheap part that halts operations gets A-level treatment regardless of its dollar rank.*

*Q2 — Turnover = 600,000 ÷ 50,000 = 12 times per year. Days of inventory = 365 ÷ 12 ≈ 30 days. Note the input is COGS, not sales revenue — using revenue would overstate turnover by the amount of your margin.*

*Q3 — X (False). The defining feature of VMI is that the reorder decision moves to the supplier, who works from shared sales and inventory data within agreed min/max levels. If the buyer is still writing the POs, it's just a responsive vendor, not VMI.*
